youtube.aciklama:
How do we plan a hearing aid fitting for an older adult? In this lesson we learn about the role of cognitive screening, how dexterity and vision affect device choice, training with the teach-back method, the caregiver's role, communication strategies and the follow-up plan.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Dillon, Hearing Aids; Weinstein, Geriatric Audiology; American Academy of Audiology, Guidelines for the Audiologic Management of Adult Hearing Impairment; Nasreddine et al. (2005), The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), Journal of the American Geriatrics Society; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how to look beyond the audiogram when assessing an older adult.
We will cover cognitive screening, how dexterity and vision affect device choice, caregiver involvement and follow-up.
In an older adult, a successful fitting is planned around the whole person, not only the audiogram.
Cognitive status directly affects learning and remembering how to use a new device.
Vision determines whether the person can see a small battery, a microphone port or the text in a phone app.
Dexterity, that is, fine finger movement, determines whether the person can insert the device and change batteries.
Health problems such as joint disease, tremor or weakness after a stroke can also affect use.
Finally, we ask whether the person lives alone and who supports them in daily life.

maddeler.metin: Verbal tests are affected by hearing
Refer to a physician if concerned

yan.metin: A short screen: it *does not diagnose*, but helps decide on referral

cumleler: Cognitive screening is a short test that shows whether further assessment is needed.
Screening does not diagnose; a diagnosis is made by a physician's evaluation.

cumleler.yazi: Common screening tests such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, or MoCA, take about ten minutes.
cumleler.ses: Common screening tests such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, or Moka, take about ten minutes.

cumleler: However, most of these tests rely on spoken instructions, and a person who answers a question they did not hear scores lower.
Using a personal sound amplifier, a quiet room and written instructions during the test reduces this error.
Screening versions adapted for people with hearing loss have also been developed.
If the screening result raises concern, the person is referred to a physician for evaluation, with their consent.
The result also shapes device choice and counseling: a simpler device and more caregiver involvement may be needed.

maddeler.metin: Very small device, very small battery

cumleler: The smallest in-the-canal devices may look attractive, but a very small body and battery are hard for older fingers.
The smallest battery sizes require fine dexterity and good vision.
Rechargeable devices remove the need to change batteries; the device is placed in its charger every night.
Behind-the-ear or receiver-in-canal devices can offer a larger body and clearer buttons.
Whether to use an earmold or a dome is also chosen for ease of insertion; some people guide an earmold more easily.
The most reliable method is to have the person insert, remove and charge the device with their own hands in the clinic.
The color code on the devices, red for right and blue for left, prevents mixing up the ears.
For people with poor vision, small markers that can be found by touch can be added to the device or the charger.
Good lighting and a magnifier make cleaning and filter changes easier.
Written instructions should be in large print, illustrated and step by step.
If a phone app is used, the text size is enlarged and only the necessary functions are shown.
Vision loss also weakens lipreading, so supporting hearing is even more important for these people.

sahneler.baslik: Why do devices end up *in a drawer?*
cumleler: Some devices of older users are known to stay unused in a drawer; one of the most common reasons is difficulty of use.
Unmet expectations in noisy settings are another reason for disappointment and giving up.
Comfort problems such as itching, pressure, a muffled own voice or whistling shorten wearing time.
Some people worry that the device will make them look old.
Most of these barriers can be solved with regular follow-up and small adjustments; the problem is often the process, not the device.
So talking openly about these barriers with the person at the first visit is the first step to preventing later abandonment.

maddeler.metin: Fit to target, verify by measurement

cumleler: For older adults too, the device is fitted to the target of a prescriptive formula and verified with real ear measurement.
For a first-time user, gain can start a little below target during acclimatization and be increased gradually.
But this is a temporary step; staying far below target for a long time reduces the audibility of speech.
Keeping few programs and automatic switching reduces the number of actions the person has to remember.
For the telephone, television and meetings, supports such as a telecoil or a remote microphone are considered.
It is explained in advance that speech in noise may still be hard with the device; realistic expectations increase satisfaction.
In training, one skill at a time is explained in short, simple language.
Then the skill is shown slowly; using a mirror helps with inserting the device.
Next the person does the same task with their own hands; the audiologist helps only when needed.
In the last step, the person is asked to explain what they learned in their own words; this is called the teach-back method.
Teach-back lets us see that the person really understood, instead of assuming it.
The session ends with illustrated, step-by-step instructions to take home.
A caregiver is a family member or professional who supports the older person in daily life.
When the caregiver joins the visits, the history and goals become richer.
Training the caregiver in daily tasks such as insertion, cleaning and charging can markedly increase use.
The caregiver is also often the one who puts communication strategies into practice at home.
The caregiver can observe how much the device is used and when problems arise, and report this at follow-up.
People with cognitive decline may swallow button batteries; batteries and devices should be stored away from them and from children.
The caregiver's own burden should not be overlooked; a simple, sustainable plan is better for everyone.

maddeler.metin: Face to face, light on face
Get attention first, use their name
Reduce noise, turn off the TV

cumleler: When talking, face the person and let the light fall on the speaker's face, so lip and facial cues can be seen.
Before starting to speak, get the person's attention by calling their name.
Before important conversations, the television or radio is turned off, and a quiet corner is chosen if possible.
A sentence that was not understood is said again in other words rather than repeated exactly.
Important information, such as an appointment time, is checked by briefly asking whether it was understood correctly.
These strategies do not replace the device; used with it, they make taking part in social life easier.
A short phone call in the first days after fitting catches small problems before they grow.
At the check in the first weeks, comfort, sound quality and handling problems are addressed and fine-tuning is done.
The device's data logging objectively shows daily hours of use and the settings in which it was used.
If use is low, the reason is explored with curiosity, not blame; there is often a solvable barrier.
After a few months, outcomes are assessed with standard questionnaires and the person's own goals.
After that, a check of hearing and the device at least once a year is recommended; needs can change with age.
For people living in care homes, device use depends largely on staff, so staff training is critical.
Name labels and a fixed storage place are practical steps to keep devices from getting lost.
For people with dementia, the aim is to ease communication with the simplest use and strong caregiver support.
In these people, better communication can reduce agitation and make daily care easier.
Older adults with profound loss and too little benefit from hearing aids can be evaluated for a cochlear implant; age alone is no barrier.
When hearing and vision loss occur together, working with specialists from both fields is needed.

sahneler.metin: On fitting day, do not end the visit until the person has inserted, removed and charged the device several times with their own hands. Use a mirror and written instructions.
cumleler: A tip from the field: on fitting day, do not end the visit until the person has inserted and removed the device a few times themselves.
Placing it in the charger and changing the battery or filter should also be done by the person.
A task done in the clinic with the audiologist's help may not be possible alone at home.
If a step is difficult, the device or earmold choice is reconsidered that day, solving the problem before it surfaces at home.
If the caregiver is at the visit, have them do the same steps; they become a second helper at home.

maddeler.metin: Assess cognition, vision and dexterity together
Screening does not diagnose; refer if needed

cumleler: In older adults, assessment covers cognition, vision, dexterity and living situation as well as hearing.
Cognitive screening does not diagnose; it is used keeping in mind that hearing loss can lower verbal test scores.
Device and earmold choice is based on the real skill the person shows in the clinic; rechargeable devices can make things easier.
Training with teach-back, caregiver involvement and planned follow-up keep the device in use.

sahneler.soru: What is the aim of teach-back in hearing aid training for older adults?
sahneler.aciklama: The person explains it in their own words: _understanding is seen, not assumed_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what is the aim of the teach-back method used in hearing aid training for older adults?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: to see that the person really understood.
The person explains what they learned in their own words, so a missing step is noticed and completed in the clinic.
